source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Mukamal_2019_MRCritique.pdf, online-first version (European Journal of Epidemiology, published online 24 November 2019; no printed page numbers), pp. 1-5 of the online-first PDF: all pages read in the text layer and checked on the rendered pages (header, Figure 1, section boundaries, and the end matter, which has only 'Acknowledgements None' and no funding or conflict-of-interest statement). An essay with no data of its own and no supplement.

claims.overstatement: 'Genetic studies do not find the lower risk' is broader than this source allows. The essay reports that several East Asian genetic reports (its refs 17-19, not read) found higher coronary heart disease risk in carriers of the drinking-lowering ALDH2 rs671 variant, which on an instrumental reading points the other way (those authors did not infer a benefit from alcohol), and it argues that genetic results may reflect binge drinking rather than average intake. 'The genetic studies read do not find the lower risk' would be accurate.
claims.note: Mukamal et al. give no figures; they support only the sentence that the causal question is disputed (status contested is consistent with this source). Every number in this claim comes from other sources.

anchors.extracted: Genetic results on alcohol are inconsistent: the China study (genetic and area-based instruments combined) reported dose-dependent harm for stroke and no effect on myocardial infarction, while several other East Asian reports found higher coronary heart disease risk with the ALDH2 rs671 variant, which lowers drinking; those authors did not infer a causal benefit from alcohol, a reading the essayists call appropriate.

Drinking has three partly correlated dimensions (frequency, usual quantity per occasion, binge drinking); drinking-lowering variants reduce all three, so genetic analyses cannot separate them, and studies linking such variants to lower cardiovascular risk may be showing the harm of binge drinking.

anchors.page: pp. 1 and 4 of the online-first PDF
anchors.extracted: The authors hold that genetic instrumental analysis is fundamentally observational, open to confounding, weak-instrument bias, pleiotropy, adaptation and failure of replication, and that the alcohol and cardiovascular example needs the caution owed to all observational epidemiology; they urge dropping 'randomization' and causal terms.

Variants act from birth, so the analyses compare lifelong (and parental) exposure; given heavy drinking patterns in adolescence and early adulthood, they may be testing young-adult binge drinking, with uncertain relevance to limited intake in mid-life.

claims.overstatement: None. Minor: 'three epidemiologists' is not stated in the source, which gives affiliations only (Department of Nutrition, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health; Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston).
claims.note: Each of the six arguments listed is in the essay: ancestry (Confounding, 1st-2nd paragraphs), parents' genes and drinking (Confounding, 3rd), weak gene-intake link (Weak instrument bias, 1st-2nd), acetaldehyde rather than amount (Pleiotropy, 2nd), heavy drinking days (Pleiotropy, 3rd), lifelong rather than adult drinking (Adaptation, 1st-2nd). 'They quantify none of these and report no figures from the studies they criticize' confirmed: the only numbers are the share of Ashkenazi Jews in Europe's population (about 0.2%), 3-5 principal components and a Google-interest chart (Figure 1). 'No funding or interests statement printed' confirmed (p. 4: Acknowledgements none; no other end matter). The essay gives no instrument-strength statistic and no sensitivity analysis; its weak-instrument argument rests on the ADH1B genotype not being associated with HDL cholesterol in Holmes et al. although alcohol raises HDL in trials. The claim omits one argument that bears on its genetic summary: inconsistent genetic results, including several East Asian reports (refs 17-19, not read) of higher coronary risk in carriers of the drinking-lowering ALDH2 variant (p. 4); the claim's 'none of the four genetic studies read' remains accurate as restricted, and the essay's description of the China study (no effect on myocardial infarction) agrees with the claim's Millwood figures. Status contested is consistent with this source.

anchors.extracted: Population stratification: the ADH1B rs1229984 variant is most common in people of East Asian and Middle-Eastern (including Jewish) descent; in the large ADH1B analysis it went with lower reported drinking but also with more education, likely an ancestry effect; adjustment with 3-5 principal components cannot capture a group as small as Ashkenazi Jews (about 0.2% of Europe's population), and the variant is linked to neighbouring variants.
Parental confounding: carriers of drinking-lowering variants are less likely to have been raised by parents with alcohol problems, itself a cardiovascular risk factor.

Self-reported drinking is misreported in both directions, so gene-intake associations may themselves be biased; in the ADH1B analysis the genotype was not associated with HDL cholesterol although alcohol raises HDL in trials, which the authors read as suggesting weak-instrument bias and non-alcohol pathways. No instrument-strength statistic is given.

ALDH2 rs671 raises acetaldehyde exposure among people who drink and could act directly; the stronger ADH1B associations in people who drink than in those who do not could reflect toxicity rather than less drinking. The variants lower frequency, quantity and binge drinking together, so analyses cannot separate them and may be showing the harm of binge drinking.

Genetic analyses test lifelong and parental exposure rather than adult drinking, and may be testing adolescent and young-adult binge drinking, with uncertain applicability to limited intake in mid-life.

Inconsistent genetic results: the China study reported harm for stroke and no effect on myocardial infarction, while several other East Asian reports found higher coronary heart disease risk with the drinking-lowering ALDH2 rs671 variant; those authors did not infer a causal benefit from alcohol.

Chan School of Public Health, and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center; approach called fundamentally observational, with a call to drop randomization and causal terms; Acknowledgements: none; no funding or conflict-of-interest statement printed.

claims.overstatement: None; the claim's 'may partly reflect heavy drinking days' is milder than the essay, which says such studies 'may well be proving the harm of binge drinking' (p. 3). The essay gives no figures for how far variants lower heavy drinking; the 0.78 is from Holmes et al. and correctly attributed there.
claims.note: The essay supports that this critique was made; it rests on argument, citing a review by Roerecke and Rehm (2010) for heavy drinking, rather than average quantity, being linked to cardiovascular harm (its ref. 11), and on Wood et al. (2018) for differing effects of the dimensions. Nothing in it concerns the seven-study pooled figures, the 30 g a day limit or the reference groups of the claim.

anchors.extracted: Drinking has three dimensions (frequency, usual quantity per occasion, binge drinking) that correlate only partly, binge drinking being common even where usual quantity is limited; drinking-lowering variants reduce all three, so genetic analyses cannot tell whether only quantity and binge drinking carry the cardiovascular harm seen in conventional studies (citing Roerecke and Rehm, 2010), and genetic findings of lower risk with such variants may be showing the harm of binge drinking.

Because heavy drinking is common in adolescence and early adulthood and far less so in young carriers of ALDH2 variants, and binge drinking may start atherosclerosis, genetic analyses may be testing adult and even teenage binge drinking rather than limited intake in mid-life.

reporting_issues.note: The region is stated in the text, which calls it worldwide interest (Introduction, 2nd paragraph, p. 1 of the online-first PDF); query strings and scaling are not given. Each series reaches 100 at its own peak (Causality about 2011, MR about 2018; checked on the rendered p. 2), so the two appear to be scaled separately: the figure shows the trend within each term, not their relative levels. The rest of the issue stands.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high, following the worst domains (no search or selection; one-sided case). The affiliations note is borne out by the reference lists of the other two sources I read: Rimm and Stampfer on Di Castelnuovo et al.'s refs 1 and 4, Stampfer on its ref. 35, and Mukamal on Ronksley et al. (2011), Dai et al. (2015) and van de Luitgaarden et al. (2020) in Stockwell et al. (2024).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract says the alcohol example demonstrates the need for circumspection, but the essay shows only that the biases are possible; none is quantified, and no estimate or instrument-exposure association from the criticized studies is reported. Its central methodological point (genetic instrumental analysis is observational) is sound.

missed: Minor, appraisal of the essay's own evidence: the premise that drinking-lowering variants reduce the risk of alcohol dependence (Confounding, 3rd paragraph, p. 3 of the online-first PDF) rests on one 1997 study of ADH and ALDH polymorphisms in four ethnic groups in China (ref. 4), indirect for an argument about ADH1B in European-descent studies.
